validated_results.title: Alcoholic beverages and prostate cancer in a prospective US cohort study.
validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort study investigating the association between dietary alcohol consumption and incident prostate cancer risk in 294,707 men.

extraction.population: NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study participants aged 50-71 years

sample_size.excerpt: In 2 other cohort studies, white wine ( 13 ) and liquor ( 14 ) were associated with an increased prostate cancer risk, but there was no association with any of the other forms of alcohol. In this study, we prospectively examined whether alcohol consumption affected prostate cancer risk for 294,707 men enrolled in the Diet and Health Study cosponsored by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and AARP (formerly, the American Association of Retired Persons).
sample_size.location: MATERIALS AND METHODS, Study population, paragraph 1

cases.excerpt: Of the 17,227 men diagnosed with prostate cancer, 1,818 died from causes other than prostate cancer, most often other cancers or cardiovascular disease (∼40% for each).
cases.location: MATERIALS AND METHODS, Cohort follow-up and identification of cancer cases, paragraph 2

effect_size.excerpt: However, a recent analysis of 18 pooled prospective studies did not find an association between either testosterone or estradiol and prostate cancer risk ( 27 ), and there was no improvement in prostate cancer survival among men consuming at least 50 g of alcohol per day (HR = 1.35, 95% CI: 0.83, 1.21) or men reporting drinking daily (HR = 0.76, 95% CI: 0.51, 1.14) in a similar cohort study of health professionals ( 9 ).

confidence_interval.excerpt: For example, hazard ratios for men consuming ≥3 drinks daily compared with nondrinkers were similar for those who reported having received a PSA test (hazard ratio (HR) = 1.15, 95% CI: 1.04, 1.27), those not tested (HR = 1.19, 95% CI: 0.97, 1.47), and those whose PSA status was unknown (HR = 1.22, 95% CI: 1.11, 1.33).

design.excerpt: This report investigated the association between alcohol use and prostate cancer risk in a prospective cohort study of 294,707 US men aged 50–71 years in 1995–1996.

timing.excerpt: We prospectively examined whether alcohol consumption affected prostate cancer risk for 294,707 men enrolled in the Diet and Health Study cosponsored by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and AARP

continent.excerpt: Questionnaires were mailed to AARP members who were aged 50–71 years in 1995–1996 and residing in one of 8 US states (California, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania).
continent.location: MATERIALS AND METHODS, Study population, paragraph 1

exposure_measurement.excerpt: The baseline questionnaire contained items about demographics, medical history, smoking, race, education, and physical activity, as well as a food frequency questionnaire of 124 items.
exposure_measurement.location: MATERIALS AND METHODS, Data collection, paragraph 1
